idea.why: Each concern owned by exactly one node rather than smeared across three. The sharpest judgement call is splitting presentation in two: the model writes only the card sections while the deterministic shell owns doctype, CSS and header, so styling cannot drift run to run. Small miss: agents emit JSON by prompt discipline alone.

structure.why: Well chosen types and a proportionate count. The demerit is node choice at the top: all three are tool-less single-turn prompt-to-JSON calls, which is a chain's job, since the agent node adds scaffolding nothing here uses.

connections.why: The visibly weak dimension. The calendar request is parked behind a model round-trip for no data reason. There is no Merge anywhere, and the editor reaches backwards with a reference that only resolves because of the artificial serialisation. A depth of nine where five would do is the direct cost.

answer.why: A reader would recognise their request, and the calendar reaches into tomorrow, which is what a morning briefing actually needs. Delivery as a draft is defensible and deliberately non-auto-sending, but a slightly awkward answer to dashboard. Escaping is delegated to the prompt, so a stray angle bracket lands straight in the rendered markup.

appraisal: The shape is right and shows real judgement: three narrowly scoped agents, one shared model, Aggregate instead of a Code node, and a template node that owns the styling so the model only writes the card bodies. Where it falls down is the wiring: two independent fetches chained into a single nine-node line, so the calendar call sits behind a model round-trip it has no dependency on, and the briefing agent has to reach backwards because there is no Merge to rejoin at. Secondary weaknesses: tool-less agent nodes where chains would fit, and contracts enforced only by prompt wording. The first change is to fan out and merge; the second is to attach structured parsers.
